clue.text: The winner of his cycling heat ?

definitions.text: The winner of his cycling heat ?

parts.words: The winner of his cycling heat
parts.note: read the clue as a racing cyclist who tears along fast enough to win his heat, with heat also hinting at a blazing hot day

explanation.surface: A question about who took first place in a qualifying round of a bike race.
explanation.walkthrough: A scorcher was old slang for a reckless fast cyclist; the word also means a very hot day, which 'heat' teases.
explanation.definitionFit: Early cycling slang named a speeding rider by this word, and such a rider wins races.

clue.text: Disappointment, seeing French cat endlessly ape a Cheshire one

indicators.note: endlessly says the final letter of the French word is cut off

parts.note: chat is the French word for cat
to copy the cat from Alice in Wonderland is to smile broadly, its famous feature

explanation.surface: Feeling let down as one watches a French feline imitate the cat from Alice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endlessly' drops the T of CHAT, leaving CHA; 'a Cheshire one' points back to 'cat', so aping a Cheshire cat means grinning.
explanation.definitionFit: Chagrin is annoyance or distress at having failed or been humiliated.

clue.text: Might a boxer use such skill in wooing ?

definitions.text: Might a boxer use such skill in wooing

parts.words: Might a boxer use such skill in wooing
parts.note: a fighter's art in the boxing arena, with a hint at the skill of a suitor who offers an engagement band

explanation.surface: A question whether a prizefighter's talents help with courtship.
explanation.walkthrough: Ringcraft is a boxer's tactical skill in the ring; a wooer's craft ends with a ring for the finger.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a boxer's expertise in the arena where fights take place.

clue.text: Channel Island has that something for a recluse

parts.note: Herm is one of the small Channel Islands, near Guernsey
'it' is slang for an indefinable appeal, that special something

explanation.surface: One of the islands off Normandy offers something special for a loner.
explanation.walkthrough: HERM is a small car-free Channel Island, one of the British islands off the French coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A hermit is someone who lives alone, apart from society.

clue.text: As' one interprets various pictures, perhaps

indicators.note: various suggests different forms, so the letters of the preceding words appear in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Each person reads paintings in their own way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'various' rearranges the fifteen letters of AS ONE INTERPRETS; 'perhaps' marks pictures as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pictures are depictions, images that portray something.

clue.text: Wilkie Collins's anonymous work

parts.note: a novel by the Victorian writer whose title, read literally, describes something without a title or author's label

explanation.surface: A query about a book the Victorian novelist published without his name on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilkie Collins, author of The Woman in White, wrote a novel called No Name (1862); 'anonymous' describes the title's literal meaning, not how it was published.
explanation.definitionFit: The novel's title literally means lacking a name, which is what anonymous means.

clue.text: Starting place of an excursion to Hastings

definitions.text: Starting place of an excursion to Hastings

parts.words: Starting place of an excursion to Hastings
parts.note: the French region from which an army set out across the Channel in 1066, described as if it were a day trip

explanation.surface: Where a coach trip to the English seaside town sets off.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'excursion' was William the Conqueror's invasion of England in 1066, ending at the Battle of Hastings.
explanation.definitionFit: William the Conqueror's invasion fleet sailed from this French duchy.

clue.text: His enemies were jarred with fatal results

definitions.text: His enemies were jarred with fatal results

parts.words: His enemies were jarred with fatal results
parts.note: a tale where robbers hid in large oil vessels and were killed there, with 'jarred' read literally as put in jars

explanation.surface: A man whose foes received a shock that killed them.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Arabian Nights tale, the forty thieves hide in jars and are killed by boiling oil poured in by Morgiana.
explanation.definitionFit: The woodcutter of the Arabian Nights story was the thieves' enemy, and they died hidden in jars.

clue.text: He does the correct thing

parts.note: 'correct' read as a verb: a person who fixes errors in texts, not one who behaves properly

explanation.surface: A man who always behaves properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'correct' looks like an adjective (proper), but it is the verb: an emendator corrects texts.
explanation.definitionFit: To emend is to correct a text, and an emendator is one who does so.

clue.text: Composer involved general in war

indicators.note: in tells us the scrambled letters sit inside the word for conflict

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: involved means tangled or twisted up, so the letters of the officer's abbreviation are jumbled

explanation.surface: A musician who got caught up with a military commander during wartime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' scrambles the general's abbreviation, and 'in' places the result inside the word for conflict, splitting it after its second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Wagner was the German composer of the Ring cycle operas.

clue.text: RAF officer mixes winter drink

parts.note: PO is short for Pilot Officer, a junior Royal Air Force rank

indicators.note: mixes says the following word's letters are stirred into a new order

explanation.surface: An air force man prepares a seasonal cocktail for the cold months.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mixes' scrambles only the season's name; the Pilot Officer's abbreviation stays in front unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a fortified wine from Portugal, drunk especially after dinner.

clue.text: Standard procedure 'for piano pupils

definitions.meaning: the usual established way of doing things, as in 'normal working method'
what learners at the keyboard are told to do daily: repeated exercises and scales

explanation.surface: The routine way things are done when teaching children the piano.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both an established custom and repeated exercise to gain skill, which every music student needs.

clue.text: State of many, no doubt, in RAF raids

definitions.text: State of many, no doubt, in RAF raids

indicators.note: in signals that the answer lies inside the run of letters in the two words that follow

explanation.surface: Many people were frightened during air force bombing attacks.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across rAF RAIDs. The whole clue doubles as the definition: being frightened is the state of many during air raids.
explanation.definitionFit: Fear is the condition many people would be in when bombs fall.

clue.text: Popish queen's Indian currency?

definitions.meaning: belonging to Queen Anne under the Latin form of her name used by the poet Alexander Pope in The Rape of the Lock
old Indian coins, each worth one sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.surface: A Catholic monarch's money from the subcontinent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Popish' looks like it means Roman Catholic, but it means 'of Pope', the poet, who wrote 'great Anna! whom three realms obey'.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope called Queen Anne by a Latinate form of her name, and the old coins of British India shared that spelling in the plural.

clue.text: They killed two fools in the south

indicators.note: two tells us to write the word for fools twice in a row

parts.note: an ass is a fool
S is the abbreviation for south

explanation.surface: A pair of idiots in southern parts were murderers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'two fools' gives ASS twice, ASSASS, then IN and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Assassins are murderers, especially of public figures.

clue.text: This beggar seems incapable of reform

definitions.text: This beggar seems incapable of reform

parts.words: This beggar seems incapable of reform
parts.note: the word for a beggar split into pieces reads like someone saying they are unable to repair or improve themselves

explanation.surface: A remark that a certain vagrant will never change his ways.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as MEND I CAN'T: the beggar seems to admit he cannot reform.
explanation.definitionFit: A mendicant is someone who lives by begging, like friars of the begging orders.

clue.text: Rustic transporter takes in Mrs Swan, a woodworker

indicators.note: takes in means one word swallows the other within it

parts.note: a carter drives a cart, a country carrier of goods
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: A country carrier gives a lift to a lady called Swan, who makes furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mrs Swan' looks like a woman's name, but it is the wife of a cob, the female swan. 'takes in' puts her inside the country carrier.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter is a craftsman who works with timber.

clue.text: Machine parts lost by a lost traveller

definitions.meaning: components that let a shaft turn with little friction, such as ball races
one's sense of direction and position, which a wanderer who has gone astray has lost

explanation.surface: A lost traveller has mislaid some mechanical components.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both rotating supports in machines and one's orientation, which someone who is lost has lost.

clue.text: Sounds as if Galatea really did come to life-in a restaurant!

definitions.text: Sounds as if Galatea really did come to life-in a restaurant!

parts.words: Sounds as if Galatea really did come to life-in a restaurant
parts.note: a small sculpted figure, whose name said out loud is 'statue ate', as if the carved woman of myth became alive and dined out

explanation.surface: A fanciful report that the mythical sculpted woman was spotted eating out.
explanation.walkthrough: Galatea is the statue Pygmalion carved, which came to life; STATUETTE sounds like 'statue ate', proof of life over dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: A statuette is a small sculpted figure, and Galatea was a sculpted figure.

clue.text: Shylock said he took no interest in his business

definitions.text: Shylock said he took no interest in his business

parts.words: Shylock said he took no interest in his business
parts.note: the merchant in The Merchant of Venice whom the moneylender resented for lending money without charging interest

explanation.surface: The moneylender complained that a man was bored by his own work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'took no interest' looks like boredom, but it means charged no interest on loans, which Shylock resented in Antonio, Shakespeare's merchant of Venice.
explanation.definitionFit: Antonio is the title merchant in The Merchant of Venice who lends money gratis.

clue.text: Gloomy doctor meets auditor

parts.note: an auditor is literally a hearer, so the organ of hearing stands for it

explanation.surface: A depressed physician has a meeting with the accountant checking the books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'auditor' looks like an accountant, but here it means a listener, hence the ear.
explanation.definitionFit: Drear is a poetic form of dreary, meaning dull and dismal.

clue.text: Go ahead with a loan

definitions.meaning: money paid early or lent, as a noun

explanation.surface: Proceed with borrowing money.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to move forward and money paid before it is due.

clue.text: Odds on the downfall causing ankle trouble?

parts.note: SP is starting price, the betting odds at the start of a race
rain is literally what falls down from the sky

explanation.surface: Betting on a tumble that leads to a twisted ankle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the downfall' looks like a fall that hurts the ankle; it is rain falling. SP, the starting price, is a British betting term for odds.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprain is a wrenched joint, and the ankle is the commonest one hurt.

clue.text: Hen easy to catch

definitions.meaning: a brooding bird that stays on her eggs
a noun in the answer for an easy chance, especially a cricket ball any fielder should hold, while the clue words are an adjective phrase

explanation.surface: A chicken that is simple to capture.
explanation.definitionFit: A brooding hen sits on eggs, and cricketers call a simple catch the same word.

clue.text: Far from light-headed but of unstable equilibrium

definitions.meaning: having too much weight up top, the reverse of a light head
liable to topple because the centre of gravity is high

explanation.surface: Someone thoroughly sober yet still wobbly on their feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Something with a heavy upper part is weighted at the head and so tends to overbalance.

clue.text: Insinuation will end in 'union disruption

indicators.note: disruption means breaking up, so the two words' letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: Hints are dropped that a strike will finish when the trade union breaks apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disruption' rearranges the letters of END and UNION.
explanation.definitionFit: An innuendo is an indirect, usually suggestive or disparaging hint.

clue.text: A part-time job

parts.note: playing a role on stage is a 'part' job, and filling in temporarily is a job for a time only

explanation.surface: A description of employment that takes only some of the week.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'part' as a stage role, and 'part-time' as temporary: an acting manager holds the job only for now.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting is performing a role in a play, and the word also means serving temporarily in a post.

clue.text: Old ones get paid off with a vengeance

definitions.text: Old ones get paid off with a vengeance

parts.words: Old ones get paid off with a vengeance
parts.note: the idiom of settling long-standing grudges, with 'paid off' read as revenge rather than repaying a debt

explanation.surface: Ancient debts are finally cleared, and fiercely.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom is 'to settle old scores': to take revenge for past wrongs.
explanation.definitionFit: Grudges are called old scores, and paying them off means getting revenge.

clue.text: Trifles with axiom about natural heat

parts.note: a maxim stating what the daytime star does to wet things, put as a two-word saying

explanation.surface: Minor matters connected with a principle concerning warmth from nature.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as SUN DRIES, a self-evident truth about the sun's heat.
explanation.definitionFit: Sundries are miscellaneous small items, things of little importance.
